tldr: A safety-filtering framework based on Poisson Safety Functions (PSF) that guarantees real-time collision avoidance for both the full robot body and grasped objects without retraining Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of VLPSA. Nominal trajectories generated by an upstream VLA model are safely filtered using dual-resolution Poisson Safety Functions (PSF) constructed online from sensor point clouds and Control Barrier Functions (CBF). Upon grasping an object, sample points are injected across its surface, protecting the full robot body and the grasped object as a single unified entity.
overview:
Large-scale Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have dramatically advanced general-purpose robotic manipulation. However, imitation-learning-based policies lack geometric safety guarantees in environments outside their training distribution. Especially in cluttered and dynamic environments where robots collaborate alongside humans, the risk of collisions involving the arm links or grasped objects is constant.

To address this, the authors propose "VLPSA," a framework that provides full-body safety guarantees within the control loop at deployment (inference) time without any retraining of the VLA. By solving the elliptic partial differential equation—the Poisson equation—in real time over environmental occupancy grids, smooth safety functions (Poisson Safety Functions: PSF) are synthesized online. Using these functions, a Quadratic Program based on Control Barrier Functions (CBF-QP) is formulated, minimally modifying the nominal trajectory from the VLA into safe joint velocity commands. Furthermore, the framework introduces a multi-grid composition combining coarse and fine resolutions across the workspace, along with a mechanism that dynamically adds bounding box surface points of a grasped object to the robot's protected geometry.

On the SafeLIBERO simulation benchmark, VLPSA dramatically increased the collision avoidance rate of the base $\pi_{0.5}$ policy from 23.1% to 91.2%, outperforming existing safety-filtering baselines. Real-world experiments on a Franka FR3 arm confirmed that the full body and grasped objects reliably avoid collisions in real time, even in scenes with dense obstacles, dynamic human interference, and flying balls.
contributions: Proposed a PSF-CBF safety filter that guarantees full-body collision avoidance in dynamic, cluttered environments without requiring VLA retraining.
Constructed a multi-grid PSF via Boolean OR composition of a coarse global grid and a fine task-region grid, achieving both high spatial precision and real-time computation.
Established collision avoidance guarantees for grasped objects by dynamically injecting surface sample points of unknown grasped objects as geometric extensions of the end-effector link.
Demonstrated pick-and-place tasks under dynamic human and obstacle interference on a physical Franka FR3 manipulator within a 150 Hz safety filter control loop.

sections.heading: Why even smart VLAs need an uncompromising safety brake on the floor
sections.summary: While VLA models are achieving versatile manipulation capabilities, they lack geometric safety guarantees outside their training distributions. This work proposes a geometric safety filter that protects the full robot body and grasped objects from dynamic obstacles in real time without policy retraining.
sections.details:
Recently, VLA models such as $\pi_{0.5}$ and OpenVLA have shown impressive capabilities. However, because they rely on imitation learning, they offer no rigorous guarantees against collisions when encountering unmodeled obstacles or configurations outside their training data.

Existing approaches for safety include training on safe demonstration data, constrained reinforcement learning, and reachability analysis using world models. Yet these methods rely heavily on the representational accuracy of learned models and do not provide geometrically independent safety guarantees. Moreover, VLAs output action chunks (sets of setpoints) at low frequencies (a few Hz to tens of Hz). When a human or dynamic obstacle enters the workspace mid-execution, correcting at the chunk level introduces dangerous response delays.

To overcome these issues, this work passes the VLA trajectory through a safety filter running at control frequencies (100 Hz or higher). By combining Control Barrier Functions (CBF) and Poisson Safety Functions (PSF), geometric safety is guaranteed without retraining the policy. The core novelty lies in extending safety guarantees from the full robot arm to unknown grasped objects, alongside a multi-resolution PSF that satisfies both real-time constraints and fine-grained spatial accuracy in tight spaces.

sections.heading: Theoretical foundations: Control Barrier Functions and Poisson Safety Functions
sections.summary: This section explains the basics of CBFs for forward invariance and the mathematics of PSFs for deriving smooth barrier functions from perception data. It connects these formulations to manipulator kinematics to establish sample-based full-body safety guarantees.
sections.details:
### II-A Control Barrier Functions (CBF)
For a system state $\mathbf{x}$, the safe set is defined where a scalar function satisfies $h(\mathbf{x}, t) \ge 0$. A CBF guarantees that a state starting in the safe set remains there indefinitely (forward invariance) by enforcing $\dot{h} \ge -\alpha(h)$ on the control input. To minimally alter the nominal control input $k_{\mathrm{nom}}$, a Quadratic Program (CBF-QP) is solved. In this work, task tracking is framed as a Control Lyapunov Function (CLF); when safety conflicts with task tracking, a CLF-CBF-QP relaxes the CLF constraint via a slack variable $\delta$.

### II-B Poisson Safety Functions (PSF)
Analytically designing $h$ for arbitrary obstacle geometries is notoriously difficult. PSFs solve the Poisson equation $\nabla^2 h_0 = f < 0$ over the sensor-derived free space $\Omega$ with Dirichlet boundary conditions ($h_0 = 0$ on $\partial\Omega$). This automatically yields a smooth function that is zero on obstacle surfaces and strictly positive inside the free space. Dynamic obstacles are handled by re-solving this moving-boundary problem online.

### II-C Application to Manipulators and VLA Policies
Manipulator control is treated as a kinematic system driven by joint velocities $\mathbf{v}$. To protect the full body, a finite set of points $\mathcal{Y}(\mathbf{q})$ is sampled across the robot surface at resolution $\varepsilon$. By solving the PSF on an environment pre-buffered (dilated) by $\varepsilon$, enforcing the CBF constraint across this finite sample set mathematically guarantees collision avoidance for the entire continuous surface. Nominal action chunks from the VLA are interpolated into a continuous trajectory, tracked via the CLF, while the QP computes safe joint velocities satisfying all CBF constraints.

sections.heading: Inside VLPSA: dynamic grasp protection and dual-resolution Poisson solving
sections.summary: Details the tracking design for VLA trajectories, the sample injection method that immediately incorporates grasped objects into safety constraints, and the Boolean multi-resolution PSF composition that balances speed with narrow-gap clearance.
sections.details:
### III-A VLA + Safety Filter
Filtering individual VLA actions point-by-point risks accumulating tracking errors and losing policy intent. Instead, action chunks of size $T$ are linearly interpolated into a continuous trajectory $\mathbf{x}_d(t)$ and tracked with a CLF in a high-rate control loop. When safety constraints intervene, the CLF constraint is relaxed via slack variables, prioritizing safety above all while maintaining maximal forward task progress.

### III-B Grasp-triggered Sample Injection
During manipulation, grasping an object fundamentally alters the robot's physical geometry. Conventional learned safety filters struggle to adapt to such dynamic geometric changes. VLPSA detects the grasp time $t_g$, constructs a bounding volume $\hat{\mathcal{B}}_O^E$ around the target object in the end-effector frame, samples its surface at resolution $\varepsilon_O$, and immediately injects these points into the robot's sample set ($\mathcal{Y}_{\mathrm{aug}}$). As long as a rigid grasp is maintained, these sample points cover the object surface, extending full collision avoidance guarantees to the grasped object by theorem.

### III-C Multi-resolution Poisson
Increasing PSF grid resolution allows navigating narrow passages, but solving the PDE across a high-resolution workspace causes computation times to explode, breaking real-time reactivity to dynamic obstacles. VLPSA solves two grids in parallel: a coarse grid (resolution $\delta_c$) covering the entire workspace, and a fine grid (resolution $\delta_f$) focused on the task region. To prevent the artificial boundary walls of the fine grid from artificially driving the safety function to zero, a Boolean OR composition is applied: $h = \max(h_f, h_c)$. Rather than differentiating non-smooth maximums, two relaxed constraints smoothed by the difference $\Delta_i = |h - h_i|$ are enforced simultaneously. This eliminates discontinuity artifacts during mode transitions, ensuring smooth and safe control.

captions.F2: Multi-grid behavior analysis. The left plot shows the fine-grid selection ratio for sample points on a grasped object, demonstrating stable fine-grid usage in static clutter and sharp peaks when dynamic obstacles approach. The right plot illustrates synthesized zero-level contours, showing seamless integration between the fine grid (blue) and coarse grid (orange).

sections.heading: Proven collision avoidance performance in simulation and physical hardware
sections.summary: VLPSA achieved a 91.2% collision avoidance rate on the SafeLIBERO benchmark, surpassing baseline filters like VLSA. Real-world tests on a Franka FR3 arm validated safety in dense tabletop clutter and dynamic human/obstacle interventions.
sections.details:
### IV-A Simulation Benchmark & IV-B Simulation Discussion
Evaluations on the obstacle-dense SafeLIBERO benchmark demonstrated the method's effectiveness. While the nominal $\pi_{0.5}$ policy had a Collision Avoidance Rate (CAR) of only 23.1%, VLPSA raised it dramatically to 91.2%. Compared to the leading baseline VLSA* (77.2% CAR), VLPSA cut collision occurrences by roughly two-thirds. Disabling sample injection for grasped objects (VLPSA-NI) dropped the CAR to 78.1%, proving that protecting objects during transport is essential. Additionally, because safety filtering prevents premature episode termination caused by collisions, task success rates actually exceeded those of the nominal policy.

### IV-C Hardware Experiments
The physical setup utilized a Franka FR3 arm, two Hesai LiDARs, and two ZED2i stereo cameras.
- **Perception and Occupancy Grid**: A 1.5 m cubic workspace was maintained at 1 cm resolution. Robot self-points were masked out to prevent false detections, updating the occupancy map at over 60 Hz.
- **Sample Injection**: Upon grasping, YOLO bounding boxes were dilated and carved to produce surface samples, integrated with self-occlusion filtering.
- **Control Setup**: Coarse ($80^3$, 3 cm resolution) and fine ($50^3$, 1 cm resolution) PSFs were solved concurrently at 40 Hz, while the safety filter QP executed at 150 Hz.
- **Cluttered and Dynamic Results**: In a banana-to-bowl transport task, nominal $\pi_{0.5}$ collided with surrounding obstacles, whereas VLPSA smoothly steered through dense clutter. When humans or tossed balls abruptly entered the workspace near the arm or banana, PSF values remained positive (maintaining safety margins), and the robot autonomously resumed manipulation once the interference cleared.

The nominal VLA (top) collides with multiple obstacles, whereas VLPSA (middle) completes the task without arm or object collisions. (B) Minimum PSF evolution under repeated interventions by humans and dynamic obstacles, showing sustained positive safety margins throughout execution.

sections.heading: Conclusions and next steps: adding reliable safety to general-purpose VLAs
sections.summary: VLPSA achieves full-body and grasped-object dynamic collision avoidance without retraining VLA policies. Future directions include integration with long-horizon planners and shape-completion models robust to occlusions.
sections.details:
This work introduced VLPSA, a framework providing geometric safety guarantees for the full robot body and grasped objects during deployment of pre-trained VLA policies without retraining. Across simulations and real hardware experiments, it demonstrated high collision avoidance capabilities in dense clutter and dynamic scenarios.

For future work, the authors highlight addressing situations where safety filtering pushes the arm far from nominal trajectories, causing the VLA to lose context of its short-term goal (which could be resolved via Model Predictive Control or earlier safety integration). Another promising avenue is integrating shape completion networks to handle unobserved geometries caused by camera occlusions and blind spots.

takeaways: Inserting a geometric PSF-CBF safety filter into the control layer provides full-body dynamic collision avoidance without retraining underlying VLA models.
Injecting bounding box surface samples of grasped objects dynamically extends mathematical collision guarantees to both manipulator and payload as a single rigid body.
Boolean OR composition of global coarse and local fine grids maintains low computational overhead while enabling 150 Hz real-time control through tight spaces.
limitations: Relies heavily on the perception pipeline; safety guarantees can break down if obstacles fall into sensor blind spots or if an object slips significantly inside the gripper.
Cannot guarantee avoidance if dynamic obstacles move faster than sensor update rates or physical robot joint velocity limits.
When the safety filter significantly deviates the arm from the nominal path, the VLA may lose track of its short-term objective, leading to task stalling or failure.
